paragraphs.heading: The shape of a molecule
paragraphs.text: Molecular geometry is the way a molecule's atoms are arranged in three dimensions. It covers the overall shape as well as details such as bond lengths, bond angles and torsional angles. Shape matters because it affects how a substance reacts, how polar it is, its phase of matter, and its color, magnetism and biological activity.

paragraphs.heading: Three key measurements
paragraphs.text: A bond length is the average distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms. A bond angle is the angle formed by three atoms joined across at least two bonds. For a chain of four atoms, the torsional angle is the angle between two planes: one through the first three atoms and one through the last three. Together, these numbers fix where each atom sits.

paragraphs.heading: What sets the shape
paragraphs.text: Each atom's position depends on the kind of chemical bonds linking it to its neighbours. Underneath, the geometry comes from the quantum mechanical behaviour of electrons. In the valence bond approximation, the atomic orbitals of bonding atoms are said to merge, a process known as orbital hybridisation. The two most common bonds are sigma bonds, usually made from hybrid orbitals, and pi bonds, made from unhybridized p orbitals. Molecular orbital theory offers another view, in which the electrons are spread across the molecule.

paragraphs.heading: How shapes are measured
paragraphs.text: Molecular shapes can be found with spectroscopy and diffraction. IR, microwave and Raman spectroscopy read geometry from the way molecules vibrate and rotate. X-ray crystallography, neutron diffraction and electron diffraction work on crystalline solids, while gas electron diffraction suits small molecules in a gas. Shapes can also be calculated to high accuracy with ab initio quantum chemistry methods.

paragraphs.heading: Why cold is best
paragraphs.text: Geometries are best measured at low temperature. At higher temperatures the measured structure is an average over more of the shapes a molecule can reach. Rotation in particular is excited at fairly low temperatures, and averaging over rotational states broadens many spectra. That is why many spectroscopic results give reliable shapes only near absolute zero.

paragraphs.heading: Same atoms, different shapes
paragraphs.text: A molecule's shape can differ between a solid, a solution and a gas. Larger molecules often have several stable shapes that are close in energy, an effect called conformational isomerism. Structural isomers share a chemical formula but join their atoms in different orders, often with very different properties. Stereoisomers join atoms in the same order but point them differently in space, and they fall into two main kinds, enantiomers and diastereomers.
